- If sentiment is positive (≥0.2) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.0), model often underestimates; adjust downward bias, especially if recent prices are falling.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overshoots; apply a “cool-down” correction to prevent overreaction.
- Model shows strong upward bias in early forecast periods (e.g., first 5–10 days) when sentiment is neutral or positive — reduce initial forecast slope.
- If true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., price drops after a peak), model often fails to correct — add a “reversion buffer” to forecast mid-range.
- When sentiment is stable or low, model tends to lag behind true price movements — increase forecast sensitivity to recent history.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true price drops sharply, model is under-reacting — adjust for “sentiment-driven volatility” in forecast curve.
